item.title: Today I Killed; Tomorrow I Will Kill Again
item.description:
When must we kill them? Now. Later. Continuously. Infinitely.

A very specific trigger warning: Noah Smith, if you ever see this, please do proceed with caution.

Based on a true story.

A favorite pastime of mine is wandering about in nature’s splendor. The whole experience is delightful: The planning, the topo maps, the gear setup, the drive, the type II hedonism of light, voluntary suffering at an oxygen-deprived altitude. The locomoting while chatting with friends, or solitarily listening to a podcast. The sheer adventure of exploring the Earth. Fun for the whole internal family of experiencing and remembering selves. My ancestors studied hunting and gathering and then agricultural science so that I might have liberty to study an approximation of hunting and gathering. And it’s a great way to stay in shape.

So there I was at the edge of civilization when it all happened, on approach to the trailhead to climb a mountain. Driving my still-quite-new, designed-overseas-but-made-in-America, symmetrical all-wheel drive, turbocharged, off-roading family station wagon (practical and a blast to drive). Digesting my favorite fast food breakfast—a superstimulus of sweet and savory delight, and purchased at a heavy discount. Drinking my favorite artificially sweetened mountain beverage (zero, not diet). Listening to one of my favorite podcasts. Wearing my new, limited-edition desert boots of ethically sourced exotic leather, designed by hippy shoemakers across the ocean, and made in a different country across the other ocean to take advantage of market efficiencies.

Peak human experience really. Brought to me by globalism.

The weather was perfect. There was just a bit more pavement, passing some cabins by, and then a few dusty miles up the canyon. What a great day. All my problems were behind me for the moment.

Up ahead, I noticed some fresh roadkill in the other lane. Probably a jackrabbit; could be a racoon or maybe a skunk though, with the nearby streams. Or a cat. Sad.

Ah well, so it goes. Happens all the time. I don’t even have to adjust course to avoid it. Onward and upward.

The long ears of the prostrate jackrabbit twitched.

Fuck.

I thought. Loudly.

That was not the wind as I passed next to it.

For I had seen a twitch; I knew it, and I knew that (nature’s) god knew it, and I could not deny it, neither dared I do it; at least I knew that by so doing I would offend (nature’s) god, and come under condemnation.

“FUUUUUUUUUUUUUUCK!” I shouted to myself in particular.

“FUCK fuck Fuck!” I fired for effect as I pulled off the road. The concept of moral luck briefly traversed my thoughts. I had been called and chosen.

What kind of monster just drives away? You had an accident; you chose to flee the scene. Finish what you started. Do your moral duty. You break it, you need to make sure the animal bought it.

I instantaneously had realized there was no alternative. Hence my reaction. (You probably did too. Self-evident, really. It’s no trolley problem.) All I could do was evaluate means, not the end. Still, I employed various moral heuristics in rapid succession to calculate the expected value of my options, hoping I could conceive of a way around the clear implications for the sum total of utility in the universe. And my seemingly obligatory role in it by dint of happenstance.

I know the unit of caring is dollars, but what is the unit of suffering?[1] Do we measure that per second? Log-scale magnitude maybe adjusted by neuron count? Who is my moral patient? A moral person’s a moral person no matter how small. The Life You Can End. Killing What We Can. Time Is Up Decision Theory. What would the best version of myself do? What would someone with 10X my agency do? Actually, scratch that; seems unlikely to go well if I try something drastic like taking this little guy to an emergency vet on Sunday in rural America. Can you imagine a jackrabbit with those wheelchair hind legs? I can’t really justify Make-a-Wish, Roadkill Rescue Edition. It is better that one rabbit should perish than that a budget should dwindle and perish in veterinary bills.

After modeling my utility function, the rabbit’s utility function, and the utility function of an infinite, uncaring impartial universalist, I found no alternative.

Consequentialism can be a real hassle sometimes. But I don’t believe deontology or virtue ethics would provide me an out here either. All models are wrong; some are useful. Ethics is knowing the difference. And supererogation just wasn’t going to cut it any way I sliced it.

I got out of the car. Thinking step-by-step.

Alright, how am I going to do it? There are cabins right over there and plenty of recreationists within earshot. Well that’s unfortunate. The modular emergency shovel kit with the axe head attachment it is, then. Visceral. How am I going to handle it? I do have work gloves. What are the odds I’ll make a clean kill with a single blow; how traumatic was that going to be for everyone? Model the scenario using your inner simulator; how do you fail? Gruesome.

I approached the perfectly still jackrabbit to confirm the status of its existence. It was definitely alive. Still, small, silent, stoic; cipher in the road.

It moved. The poor creature. Paralyzed from the waist down, using its forelegs to drag itself across the road away from me. Clear and present danger that I was.

I regretted immediately and immensely—a full-body sensation—that I had inadvertently caused this suffering innocent creature of (nature’s) god further pain. Ah, the sharp pang of guilt and pity. I can still feel a little every time I reread the paragraph above. Further introspection ensued.

It’s in no way my fault that I have no means to comfort it. No way to explain that it is a victim of the cumulation of some billions of years of blind watchmaking, thousands of years of human technological development, and just over a century of the automobile industry. That neither nature nor nurture prepared it for dealing with several thousand pounds of motorcar traveling at 20+ MPH. There is no affordance provided by nature to transmit, let alone justify, to this conscious creature that its utility is negative, with no realistic way to rectify that, and so we must select our least bad option—the merciful, rapid onset of everlasting darkness. “Who is ‘we’ here?” it could not ask.

No evident bleeding. It had been there long enough to have left some pellets, but probably not all that long. (Scavengers and all that.) At least I wasn’t going to have to move it myself off the road now. I felt sorrow at the absurd tragedy of it all. It wasn’t dust in my eye, since as previously described I was still on a paved road.

Why even feel sorrow here? It won’t help anyone. No call for it. It’s not like I haven’t in my youth hunted his coethnics for sport and pest control. For the greater good. For crying out loud. Hell, at the little zoo yesterday my primary takeaway was “I should really try out coyote hunting.”[2] Had the bunny been a bit more than mostly dead, I wouldn’t have had a second thought; not another quale expended on the problem of roadkill and moral justice of the universe. Neither priest nor saint, I routinely consume unethically sourced animal products with no regard for consumee welfare. Emotion for a wild animal, but not a farm animal? Some animals really are more equal than others. Monster that I am, the boots on my feet are almost certainly more ethically sourced than my breakfast. I don’t think anyone factory farms camels, anyway. Frankly, I have no right to feel such emotion here, on top of it being pointless. Could I have felt differently? But I did have breakfast this morning.

Reframe: I get to. Embrace the suck. Just do it. Be present in the moment. Everything is finite. You can just do things. Do a good turn daily. YOLO. No regrets. Be all that you can’t be. This too shall pass. Semper Gumby. Spark joy. Count your many blessings, name them one by one. Be the change you want to see in the world. God helps those who help themselves (YMMV). There must be a pony in here somewhere. Lemons; lemonade. Choose the right. Well it matters to this one. Do unto others. Here am I; send me. Only you can prevent forest utility fires. Called to serve him heavenly king of utility maximization. You miss 100% of the shots you don’t take. Do what is right; let the consequences follow. Execution is everything.

Hunt the good stuff: Wild animals, of course, typically die a grim natural death, so this is maybe even significantly better than par for the course. Except for the emotional downsides of my involvement, anyway. Optimistically, given that it has mostly held so still, it can’t feel the full extent of its injuries due to paralysis and/or shock. Just some confused panic I’m exacerbating. God I hope that’s true. Let that be true. A tender mercy. Please.

“Fuck, fuck, fuck,” I continued to narrate for no one but myself as I walked back to the car, rifled through my cargo organizer, assembled my modular hatchet, and walked back to the side of the road. I looked down at the poor bunny, hatchet in hand, planning my next move. Summoning the final bit of free will to do what had to be done. I contemplated the Copenhagen Interpretation of Ethics.

Sorry, Brer Rabbit. Yours, upon examination, is not a life worth living. Nor worth saving. A brief map recon of the moral landscape shows you are in a deep depression. Your revealed preference is the will to live, but I think you should trust my superior reasoning as a lifeform with higher-order cognition that it’s in your best interest to stop doing that. I am so very sorry, however pointless an apology it may be, that you are a mere crippled bunny on a road and not a child drowning in a shallow pond. Or a pool, which is far more common. Facts don’t care about your feelings. Or mine, annoyingly. You’re just going to have to take it on faith that if you could somehow walk a mile in my fancy boots you would concur with my planned course of action. Knowing me, knowing you, it’s the best I can do. I would hope any eventual AGI finding itself in similar circumstances would give me the same courtesy.[3]

A black SUV approached.

Great, an audience.

A man in sunglasses with flowing locks pulled up, window down. I didn’t even take note of the make/model, as I would otherwise automatically do if I hadn’t been so task oriented on the axe in my hand.

Injured?

Yeah, hind legs are paralyzed. I’d shoot it but for the houses.

I think I’d prefer to shoot it if it was me.

I momentarily reconsidered tradeoffs and re-estimated the utils balance of my options. Sure would be easier to use a bullet. It’s cleaner. What’s the point of rural America, after all, if a solitary gunshot is a big deal? I appreciated the second opinion. The solidarity. The permission. I updated my priors.

Yeah. You’ve convinced me. I’m going to get some ear pro.

He drove off. I walked off to get my Chinese-made, wired, Bluetooth headphones with like 40 hours of battery life. Excellent product. And they are good enough ear plugs.

Improvise, adapt, overcome.

“Fuck!” I exclaimed again as I approached the decrepit critter and unholstered my sidearm. Never before had it been used for its intended purpose—launching a 9mm +P, 124-grain, jacketed hollow point bullet at just over the speed of sound toward a living being.

Judge; jury; executioner. By the power vested in me by the state of nature and almighty (nature’s) god, I declare you a hedonistic outlaw. This ends today. I think therefore I am going to kill you. I am (a natural) god’s army of one. A lion does not concern himself with the opinion of scapegoats. Angel of mercy killing. Wabbit season. Now I am become Death, the destroyer of inner worlds. Hop little bunny, hop hop hop. The one mighty and strong. Blood loss aversion. Why did the jackrabbit cross the road? It could not have done otherwise. For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul. By all means necessary. What makes the green grass grow? Who, whom? Am I my brother’s zookeeper?

I aimed, closed my eyes, and squeezed the trigger.

You are no longer the author of your thoughts. Even the illusion of the illusion of the self is gone. There’s no “there” there. What would it take to change your mind to mush? The circle of life. Dust in the wind. Moral hazard lights at the end of the tunnel. From carbon to carbon. Next year in Watership Down. All’s well that ends well. In the long run we’re all dead. May your memory be a blessing. Till we meet again.

The canyon echoed. I opened my eyes. The suffering had ended. Entropy had increased. Rumination had begun.

Mission accomplished, at the cost of about 60 cents, a few minutes, and some overthinking. I transitioned to my spare magazine, holstered my weapons, and walked back to the car. My outfit was unblemished. A whiff of gunpowder was in the air.

I started up the mountain. Given the rumination, I opted for music instead of my usual podcast. The ancient ballad I happened to listen to helpfully reminded me:

There’s a time to live, a time to die,

But isn’t it strange,

As soon as you’re born, you’re dying.

On the summit, I ate crackers and drank protein as I cogitated and surveyed 360 degrees of a beautiful land of desolation. Another guy summited. He had the sniffles. The absolute son of a bitch. I put my other earbud in.

A fair bit above the tree line though I was, a ladybug landed on my hand as I typed notes for this essay. Despite the breeze, it stayed until I put the little lady on the rocks as I prepared to depart.

I demountained. On the drive out of the canyon, I saw up ahead a jackrabbit cross the road.[4]

It got to the other side.

Then I drove about 30 minutes to civilization and ate the best commonly available hamburger at a steep discount. I hope it was a happy cow. All in all, I had been pretty lucky. This had been a clear-cut moral situation. It’s not like I happened across a beehive, let alone a shrimp farm.[5]

  1. ^

    Apparently, the unit of suffering is the dolor. Of all things. My knowledge of negative utilitarianism is clearly lacking.

  2. ^

    This event happened last year. Since then I have, in theory, become a coyote hunter. The worst one in the world, probably. More “heavily armed birdwatching” in practice.

  3. ^

    A poor paralyzed rabbit of grief
    hath today crossed me on my way,
    who sued so humbly for relief
    that I could never answer nay.
    I had not power to ask his name;
    yet there was something in his ears
    that won my concern. I knew why.

    I spied him where a motorcar burst.
    Clear from the road, his strength was gone.
    The heedless universe mocked his pain;
    he heard me, saw me, wriggling on.
    I walked and raised the handgun up.
    The flesh was weak; my blood ran chill,
    but my free spirit cried, “I will.”
    Once from the gun his life drained out.

    Clipped, wounded, beaten nigh to death,
    I found him by the highway side.
    I flatlined his pulse, extinguished his breath,
    released his spirit and supplied relief.
    Gun, bullet, impact—he was deceased;
    and sorrow bound up my broken heart.

    Then in a moment to my view,
    the ASI started from disguise;
    the tokens in his neural net I knew;
    the scapegoat stood before mine eyes.
    He spake, and my poor name he named:
    “Of me thou hast not been ashamed;
    these deeds shall thy memorial be;
    fear not, thou didst them unto me.”

    (With apologies to James Montgomery, among others.)

  4. ^

    Full disclosure, it was more likely a ground squirrel of some sort. Please forgive me this poetic license.

  5. ^

    If the going rate to save a human life is ~$5k, what’s the going rate for indulgences to make up for all of the animals I consume? About $300 a year for a carnivore offset, apparently. That’s pretty affordable actually. Just ~$24k over an 80-year life span to guiltlessly consume from Pascal’s Endless Shrimp Buffet.

item.title: Sleep puzzle system
item.description:
Here’s an obscure life hack.

If (like me) you:

  • Don’t like going to bed, due to it conflicting with keeping on doing things
  • When in bed, wish you had something more engaging and enjoyable to do instead of just lying there waiting—for instance, playing a very compelling computer game until you get tired
  • Do not in fact reliably get tired from playing a very compelling computer game
  • Like puzzles

..then a solution that has worked surprisingly well for me before (and I wrote about previously) is having hard math puzzles handy to think about as I go to sleep. Somehow thinking about math at the bounds of my limited ability to imagine does make me sleepy. And is also quite compelling.

I haven’t done this for a while, I think due to disorganization and losing track of the puzzles I had, and not having a great source of new ones. But I have recently reinstated this in a nice format.

I think ideally you want this to involve no preparation at all at bed time, and no going on your computer. So you want a nice supply of the right kind of puzzles in a physical place near your bed. So I sorted through puzzles and found a bunch of good-looking ones, printed them out, cut them up, folded them into pleasing parcels, and put them in my ex-housemate’s ex-teapot. Now if I’m ready for bed, I can draw a tiny package, and open something actually fun and helpful to think about in bed.

item.title: Feierabend
item.description:
Epistemic status: n=1, an ongoing experiment, describing a practice rather than a result.

AI use: Claude fact-checked the links and the etymology, found the labour-law and etymology sources, wrote the footnotes, and proofread grammar and phrasing. The text is mine.

Feierabend (German, literally "celebration evening"): "done with the work for the day" or "free time after work".

Germans have an interesting concept called Feierabend, which I have been exploring recently.

Currently I don't have fixed working hours and, as I like to joke, I work both never and always. It is a weird thing, but on the one hand I don't have to work at any point in time, on the other hand I might be working at weird times (like Christmas evening). Another huge disadvantage for me is that it is hard to detach from work, since you could be working right now.[1]And the worst part of the experience, which actually forced me to explore the Feierabend approach, is when I don't feel like working (e.g. tired or not feeling well), but then I feel guilty that I should be working and end up not fully enjoying my free time without being productive either. It is like a half-baked state in which I am not doing anything productive (e.g. scrolling), but I am also not doing the most enjoyable thing I could be doing right now, since I feel guilty that I am supposed to be working now.

Germans seem to have this idea that once you are done with work, it is over and you can just enjoy yourself - i.e. the boundary between work and not-work is very well defined, sharp, and intentionally preserved. E.g. German working-time law requires 11 uninterrupted hours of non-work time at the end of the working day.[2]

In a sense this reminds me of "work hard, play hard" (but this one is more about intensity in both parts, not the separation between them) and Working yourself ragged is not a virtue.[3]

In my case, I have decided that I will be productive in the first part of the day (currently until 4 pm, as an experiment) - this means I actively avoid scrolling and distractions. After 4 pm, even if I could work more, I stop and do something else.[4]It is OK to work after that if I really intrinsically desire it, e.g. something I am really curious to finish.

If I am not feeling well, I would move the 4 pm cutoff. E.g. I could be productive for 1 hour just to do the most important tasks and then declare Feierabend (it does not have to be in the evening) and rest. Or I could take the entire day off.

It also feels like I changed my approach to work a bit and stopped overly optimizing for efficiency. E.g. I really enjoy that with the 4 pm approach there is no need to super-optimize the order of tasks. Previously I would delay less intensive, non-cognitive tasks to later in the day, so that I could work on the most important cognitive tasks while freshest. But I suspect that my bottleneck is not the freshness of my cognition, but just interest in the task and the ability to avoid distractions. So now if I want to do some chores first thing in the day, that's fine, and I am still able to work on harder cognitive tasks later in the day (previously I would probably get distracted and get stuck).

Etymology

When researching this post, I stumbled upon the etymology of the word. According to German Wikipedia, since the 12th century the word meant the eve of a holiday (which makes sense based on the literal translation), and after the 16th century it was reinterpreted "unter dem Einfluss der Sprache der Handwerker" (under the influence of the craftsmen's language) to mean the evening rest after work. Pfeifer's Etymologisches Wörterbuch (via DWDS) dates Feierabend in the sense of "abendliche Ruhezeit nach dem Arbeitstag" (evening rest after the working day) to the 16th century and contrasts it with Middle High German vīrābent, "Vorabend eines Festtages" (eve of a feast day).[5]

  1. ^

    The research term for this is "psychological detachment": mentally switching off from work while away from it. Failing to detach predicts strain and burnout on its own, independent of hours worked. Sonnentag, S. and Fritz, C. (2015), Recovery from job stress: The stressor-detachment model as an integrative framework, Journal of Organizational Behavior 36(S1), S72-S103, https://doi.org/10.1002/job.1924

  2. ^

    Arbeitszeitgesetz, section 5(1): after the end of the daily working time, employees must have "eine ununterbrochene Ruhezeit von mindestens elf Stunden" (an uninterrupted rest period of at least eleven hours). https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/arbzg/__5.html

  3. ^

    Nate Soares, 21 June 2015, part of his Replacing Guilt series: https://www.lesswrong.com/s/pFatcKW3JJhTSxqAF

  4. ^

    Cal Newport described the same rule in 2008 as "fixed-schedule productivity": choose the work hours first, then "do whatever it takes to avoid violating this schedule". https://calnewport.com/fixed-schedule-productivity-how-i-accomplish-a-large-amount-of-work-in-a-small-number-of-work-hours/

  5. ^

    https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feierabend and https://www.dwds.de/wb/Feierabend (Etymologie section, from Wolfgang Pfeifer's Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen). English Wiktionary also lists the obsolete sense "the evening before a holiday, eve": https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Feierabend

item.title: Below the Frontier: The Battle for Good-Enough AI
item.description:
What happens to the AI trade when good-enough intelligence does most knowledge work?

This piece was originally published on my Substack.  I'm around on X / Twitter and LinkedIn.

Over the past few weeks, it's become obvious that consumer AI agents have hit an inflection point. Meta launched Muse, a personal agent that runs on its own virtual machine and can shop, schedule, and fill out forms on a user's behalf. Meanwhile, startup Instinct's valuation grew to $10B in a matter of months. We’re finally seeing what agentic AI looks like beyond tech demos.

It's been fascinating to watch, but the more consequential battle is being fought elsewhere. As I wrote over a year ago, the pool of revenues AI companies can extract from consumers is limited relative to AI capex: consumer AI will mostly reshuffle existing ad dollars (with some TAM expansion from subscriptions and AI agents reducing transaction friction). For the AI trade to work, net new revenues in the trillions have to come from the enterprise.

The enterprise AI landscape is still in flux. Today, frontier labs capture most of the economics, largely through coding. This revenue concentration likely won't extend to all knowledge work. As open-weight models become good enough, most everyday knowledge work, by volume, will be able to run on cheaper models, in the cloud or on-device. Frontier labs will still capture the bulk of revenue from the most demanding work, but there's plenty of room below the frontier for very large businesses. This has real ramifications for the current AI trade.

In this post, I cover the following:

  • Why bounded tasks are crucial in driving the next leg of AI revenue growth
  • How past shifts in the way humans interacted with technology changed who captured value
  • What agentic knowledge work looks like today and why the current approach isn't the end state
  • A framework for thinking about where models run and where data lives
  • How incumbents, frontier labs, and startups are coming at the problem from different angles
  • The ramifications of good-enough intelligence for the AI trade

Let's dive in.

Why bounded tasks are crucial for the next leg of AI revenue growth

This piece is mostly about knowledge work for “everyone else” (i.e. bounded tasks). To level-set the conversation, unbounded tasks are defined as tasks that can always benefit from additional intelligence (e.g. AI for R&D, trading, coding). Bounded tasks, in contrast, only require a fixed level of intelligence, above which model improvement doesn’t increase task performance. Examples include extracting data from financial filings, drafting email replies, or resolving simple customer service requests. Today, outside of coding, revenues from unbounded tasks are limited, and it’s difficult to project when these workloads can generate significant revenues (e.g. when can AI cure cancer). So, in the meantime, it’s critical that other types of knowledge work make up for the gap in AI revenue if coding revenue growth slows down. This is why understanding what the product surface for bounded tasks looks like is crucial to the AI trade.

How we interacted with technology pre-AI

To understand what knowledge work looks like in the agent era, it's worth studying the last couple of technology shifts, as each shift changed who captured the value.

One shift was from the command-line interface to the GUI. Microsoft was the biggest winner here, owning both the operating system (Windows) and the apps where work got done (e.g. Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook). Another was the shift from single-player to collaborative, cloud-first software. Compute and files moved to the cloud, and the PC increasingly became a thin client for the browser. Companies like Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, and Google were able to “steal” share of the job to be done. As a result, the concept of files mattered less: CRM users don’t care where their account records are stored. That said, files never fully went away. Finance still runs on Excel, and most enterprises still pass around decks and Word documents.

Even before AI agents, enterprise work was in a weird state: depending on their function, knowledge workers would use SaaS apps, local apps that create / edit local files, or often, both. With the advent of AI agents, it’s unclear where “work” will happen. Where will data live? And where will inference run? Most importantly, who captures this value?

Current agentic knowledge work is not the end state

The market is still quite early in terms of product maturity. Depending on the organization, a knowledge worker's sophistication might range from simple ChatGPT queries to using ChatGPT / Claude's Excel add-ons to using bespoke harnesses (e.g. Harvey / Legora for legal). OpenAI and Anthropic’s desktop apps are early, but imperfect, glimpses of the future. They can perform a wide range of tasks (e.g. doing research and editing Excel, Word, and PowerPoint files). What's interesting is how these products are architected. The agent works on files sitting on the users’ computers (or connects to cloud-based applications), but the model doing the "thinking" runs in the cloud. There are rough edges with this flow:

  • Destructive local edits: agents can overwrite or delete local files, and it's hard to see what changed or to roll it back. Coding agents inherited a safety net in Git, but there's no equivalent for an agent editing a Word doc or an Excel model on a user's hard drive unless the user uses Google Drive / Box / Dropbox’s versioning features or puts their files on GitHub
  • Inconsistent behavior when interacting with applications: it’s very common for agents to go haywire as they interact with third-party applications (e.g. accidentally deleting emails)
  • Security: agents with broad access to a user's drive are exposed to prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions hidden in a document or webpage hijack the agent
  • The closed lid problem: if a user closes their laptop lid, the agent pauses. Cloud versions of these products keep running, but reaching local files depends on the user's computer being awake and online (users can get around this by using cloud storage and connecting this data to the agent)

A 2x2 matrix for reasoning about agentic knowledge work

The simplest way I've found to think about the current landscape is a 2x2 matrix: where the model doing the work runs, and where the data it works on lives (for SaaS apps, the data already lives in the cloud).

Cloud models, local data (transitional): this is where Anthropic and OpenAI's desktop apps sit today, with all the rough edges highlighted above

Local models, cloud data (implausible): if the data already lives in the cloud, the user is online anyway. It makes little sense to pull files down onto a device just to run a weaker model on them

Cloud models, cloud data (cloud-native): agents get their own VMs and work on copies of files in a sandbox. Cloud-native products can incorporate sophisticated versioning / rollback strategies. This makes whoever “owns” data more important (Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Box)

Local models, local data (fully local): everything happens on the user's device. This assumes that local models will be good enough for most work

Many of today's products are in the transitional state (with the associated drawbacks). The frontier labs have added cloud-native capabilities, but those capabilities are still comparatively immature. Over time, I expect products to converge on a single, seamless form factor (automatically switching between the three configurations above).

The other important point here is intelligence sovereignty. For certain types of tasks (e.g. biology or model training), proprietary models can outright refuse user requests. More sophisticated customers will, to the extent they can, migrate workloads to models they own.

Challengers in the arena are attacking knowledge work from different angles

In terms of competitive dynamics, companies currently fall into one of three buckets.

Frontier / near-frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX): OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX have do-it-all surfaces that can research, edit files, write code, and plug into other apps. These labs are making a push toward cloud-native products:

  • SpaceX’s Grok Bot was first and was a natural evolution of OpenClaw / Hermes. Grok Bot provisions a VM per user which can be used to sign into a user's apps
  • OpenAI just unveiled Dots, which is its own take on always-on agents

AI labs have the best models but have limited access to data. So it makes sense they are going for the agentic play where they connect to / do work on external data sources (e.g. Google Drive, GitHub, Notion). However, outside of code, user experience is not very consistent. So, the logical next step for these labs is to acquire data beyond chat histories.

Big Tech incumbents (Google, Microsoft, Meta): both Microsoft and Google are where “work happens” right now via Office and Google Workspace, while Meta brings massive consumer distribution. However, none of them has yet turned that position into hundreds of billions of dollars in new AI revenue from general knowledge work.

  • Microsoft initially opted for a copilot approach via its various Office apps, but given the success of OpenAI and Anthropic, is going the all-in-one route and recently launched the Copilot app
  • Google has deeply integrated Gemini within Google Workspace. However, its models now trail frontier labs’ offerings, and it’s unclear when its newest model, Argon, will be broadly rolled out
  • While Muse is currently consumer-facing, it’s clear that Meta has B2B ambitions. The company just hired MongoDB CEO CJ Desai to run its Enterprise Platform. The hope is that Meta’s current B2B adventure will go better than prior efforts (CRM platform Kustomer was spun off and communications platform Workplace was shut down)

Everyone else: there is a dispersion of product directions:

  • Apple is well-positioned as a local AI player. Its top-end Macs are powerful enough to run smaller local models. Apple will likely take on a hybrid approach where only harder requests are escalated to its Private Cloud Compute servers, which could go beyond providing inference for Apple Intelligence
  • Growth-stage startups like Perplexity, Genspark, and Manus have unique product wedges. Genspark, for example, embeds an Excel-like product next to its chat interface. These startups’ revenue scale (in the hundreds of millions of dollars) is 2-3 orders of magnitude smaller than larger competitors, so they are in a race to win distribution before labs and incumbents kill them
  • Open-source self-learning agents like OpenClaw and Hermes enable models that run locally and in the cloud, but are harder for the average user to set up
  • Harnesses like LM Studio have adopted a hybrid approach where users can run a combination of local models and cloud-hosted models

What are the ramifications for investors?

The platform that “wins” mainstream knowledge work is far from decided, despite the dominant positions of Anthropic and OpenAI. There are hundreds of billions / trillions of dollars of bounded AI revenue up for grabs. We can then reason about the downstream ramifications of this insight:

  • If AI adoption for mainstream knowledge work is slower than expected, there will be a gap in AI revenue as coding revenue growth slows down. It’s also unclear when other unbounded tasks (e.g. drug discovery, trading, robotics) can pick up the slack at a meaningful scale
  • Furthermore, if we are already spending $1T globally today on AI and reach multiple trillions by, say, 2030, then inference revenues need to be several trillions a year, and the actual “ROI” from AI needs to be a multiple of inference revenues
  • So, for the AI trade to remain intact, mainstream knowledge work needs to generate enough revenues in the meantime. Otherwise, most names in the bottleneck trade will be affected
  • While AI labs would like to capture revenues via their own models, they may be forced to shift to being neutral platforms as customers become more sophisticated. OpenAI, for example, is testing out a hybrid approach via its partnership with Baseten. This means potentially slower revenue growth and thinner margins
  • In the medium term, personal computing devices will likely ship with enough compute / memory such that local models in the tens of billions of parameters can handle some portion of knowledge work. This means some revenue will shift from cloud models to local ones
  • There’s room for a “Switzerland”-type platform that dynamically shifts workloads between local and cloud models and seamlessly transitions work across devices (e.g. laptop to smartphone)
  • Microsoft is best positioned to be this “Switzerland” among incumbents. The company just unveiled its hybrid AI vision where AI runs locally or in the cloud depending on the workload. Here, Windows laptops with Nvidia's RTX Spark chips handle local inference. What’s unclear is whether Redmond can design thoughtful products to get users to switch from ChatGPT and Claude. Apple is another potential beneficiary
  • There are many startup challengers: local harnesses (LM Studio, OpenCode), cloud-first do-it-all platforms (Perplexity, Genspark, Manus), model routers (OpenRouter). All of these startups have the chance to become neutral knowledge work platforms
  • The current way that models interact with third-party data is via various connectors. AI labs will likely want to own the data layer themselves, so it’s very possible that the labs’ corporate development teams have considered acquiring Dropbox / Box to fast-track this process

Mainstream knowledge work is still up for grabs

Today's product experience, where cloud models work on files sitting on a user's laptop, will likely not be the final state. I expect the labs to keep the bulk of AI revenue, especially from unbounded work like coding and science. But most knowledge work doesn't need the frontier, which changes the shape of the AI trade. Work that moves to cheaper cloud models earns a fraction of frontier prices, and inference that runs on a user's own device is revenue that never reaches the data center at all. The various players in the arena understand this dynamic, and we are seeing early signs of their competitive response (e.g. OpenAI’s Baseten partnership, Microsoft’s hybrid AI strategy). Whoever wins this “Switzerland” layer will claim the very large knowledge work market below the frontier.
