item.title: When are safe Pareto improvements individually rational?
item.description:
(Soft prerequisites: A high-level model of AI bargaining and Taboo “equilibrium”: Less confused frames for research on AI bargaining.)

Section II.1 of CLR’s safe Pareto improvements (SPI) agenda briefly reviews the challenges for making SPIs individually rational. Here, I’ll flesh out these challenges, taking renegotiation SPIs as a running example. The ideas here overlap a lot with DiGiovanni et al. (2024) and its distillation. But this post will hopefully be more accessible, and will consider bargaining problems with non-simultaneous commitments. I’ll also revisit some controversial arguments made in those previous writings.

My aim is to precisely yet informally answer: “Why might an agent expect opting out of SPIs to have better consequences? What are the mechanisms leading them to expect this?” The high-level mechanisms I’ll discuss apply to a variety of SPIs, not just renegotiation, though the details importantly differ between different SPIs. I’m not confident that this list of mechanisms is exhaustive. Rather, the point is to show that at least these obstacles need to be overcome in order for SPIs to be individually rational.

See Appendix I for a table of this post’s notation, and Appendix II for how the analysis maps onto the agenda’s breakdown of “Risks 1-3”.

Summary: Consider some bargaining interaction between Alice and Bob. When would Bob prefer to agree to a given SPI with Alice? Here’s a sketch of what this post will argue:

  • Typically, SPIs work by keeping each agent’s demands the same as if the other agent hadn’t participated in the SPI, holding fixed their chosen bargaining commitments. But this isn’t sufficient for Bob to prefer agreeing to the SPI. Bob might expect that if he commits to refuse SPIs, he can get a better deal, by either (more):
    • (i) removing Alice’s incentive to choose a more demanding commitment because she expects the SPI to make bargaining failure less costly;
    • (ii) signaling to Alice that he’d make aggressive demands; or
    • (iii) refusing this particular SPI to get Alice to accept his preferred SPI (the SPI selection problem).
  • Problem (i) can be blocked if, at the time the agents bargain, it’s verifiable to Bob that Alice satisfies a weak form of participation independence (PI): her demands are no higher than those of the commitment she’d have chosen had Bob committed to unconditionally refuse SPIs. (more)
  • But even if Alice satisfies weak PI, problem (ii) remains: If Bob is still uncertain whether Alice is committed to weak PI when he chooses his own commitment, he might commit to unconditionally refuse SPIs to signal aggressiveness. (That said, this incentive appears relatively conjunctive, once we dig into the details. And it can be blocked if Alice makes her commitment to weak PI credible to Bob before he commits.) (more)
  • Even if problems (i) and (ii) are solved, the SPI selection problem (iii) remains. While there are some proposed solutions — in particular, DiGiovanni et al.’s (2024) “Pareto meet minimum”-based approach, and Oesterheld & Conitzer’s (2022) — I don’t think any are very robust, based on our current understanding. So research into mitigations of the SPI selection problem seems particularly important. (more)

Setup

Recap: Renegotiation SPIs

We’ll focus on SPIs implemented via renegotiation programs, and for simplicity we’ll just consider two agents. Renegotiation programs roughly work like this: By default, use whichever bargaining strategy you like — the same strategy regardless of whether the other agent also uses a renegotiation program. But, if the other agent also uses a renegotiation program, and your programs agree on some outcome that (weakly) Pareto-improves on the default outcome, take that outcome instead.

More precise definition. As discussed here, a bargaining program is a commitment to behavior in a bargaining problem conditional on the other agent’s program/commitment. Now, take any “default” program that an agent might use. The agent chooses some renegotiation function , which, conditional on the other agent’s renegotiation function, maps each possible bargaining outcome to a weak Pareto improvement. Then, they can construct a corresponding renegotiation program via the algorithm below: [1]

We’ll say that two programs “renegotiate” with each other if they each run line 6 of Algorithm 1 (or, an algorithm that matches Algorithm 1 except that line 5 includes additional conditions besides matching proposals; [2] this possibility will be important later). In that case, we call the outcome the programs go to the renegotiation outcome.

SPIs via renegotiation programs. Recall the agenda’s definition of SPIs (with new notation):

An SPI is a transformation such that, for all [program pairs] in some space , the agents’ payoffs [in the given game] when they all follow programs (weakly) Pareto-dominate their payoffs when they all follow .

Then we have a straightforward way to construct SPIs, given credible conditional commitment ability: Take some renegotiation function . For any given pair of programs the agents might use, map to the pair of Algorithm 1 instances with and . This mapping is an SPI, simply because maps any given outcome to a Pareto improvement.

“Default demands” of renegotiation programs. The hard part is to argue that the agents individually prefer to use such an SPI. Going forward, we’ll look at how the agents’ preferences to renegotiate depend on the demands they expect each other to make. For convenience, we’ll let an agent’s “demands” — as a quantity — refer to the payoff they get if the counterpart concedes to their demands-in-the-qualitative-sense, e.g., “give me 60% of the pie”. Then, for a renegotiation program Alice might use and any program Bob might use, let ’s default demands be the demands that makes when the two programs run against each other. See footnote for more. [3]

Problem setup

We’ll use the framework from “A high-level model of AI bargaining”. Let and be Alice’s and Bob’s respective programs. Suppose:

  • Before the bargaining phase (recall the definition here), Alice commits to renegotiation, meaning, she commits to the constraint that will be a renegotiation program.
  • Bob might choose before or after Alice commits to renegotiation. We don’t assume Bob knows Alice is committed to renegotiation when he chooses .

Then: Under which conditions would Bob prefer to use a that ends up renegotiating with Alice?

Naïvely, we might think the following argument is enough: Against any non-renegotiating program Bob might use, Alice’s renegotiation program plays (line 10 of Algorithm 1). Whereas against a renegotiation program with , her default program runs against (line 2), i.e., it again plays . So her default demands are exactly the same whether or not Bob renegotiates. [4] And the renegotiation function will make neither agent worse off. So wouldn’t Bob always prefer to have be willing to renegotiate?

But that’s too quick. We’ve only established that Bob prefers to renegotiate holding two things fixed: Alice’s default demands against both renegotiators and non-renegotiators, and the outcome they’d renegotiate to. What if Bob is uncertain of these default demands when choosing , and expects that his choice could change them? And what if Bob insists on a different renegotiation proposal (line 4 of Algorithm 1) from Alice’s?

To crudely summarize, Bob might choose a program that doesn’t renegotiate with Alice’s if he expects any of the following (not necessarily exhaustive): [5]

  • If he’s committed not to renegotiate, then:
    • Alice will lose the incentive to make high demands that renegotiation would’ve otherwise given her; or
    • Alice will take the information “Bob doesn’t renegotiate” as a signal that Bob will make high demands (and hence she won’t make high demands herself).
  • If he’s committed to renegotiate only to outcomes that are sufficiently favorable to him, then: Alice’s program will renegotiate to a better outcome for Bob than if he’d been willing to renegotiate to less favorable outcomes.

We’ll run through different cases to see when each of these possibilities might (not) apply. (See footnote for some notes on scope. [6] )

First possibility: Preempting the incentive to make higher demands

To start, suppose Bob decides whether to credibly commit to never renegotiate. We’ll call the set of programs under this constraint . Then one possible scenario is:

  • Bob thinks Alice’s default demands will be higher in expectation if his program is sometimes willing to renegotiate than if he commits to . [7] Specifically, he expects that both:
    • Alice might verify whether he’s committed to before she commits to her default demands; [8] and
    • If he doesn’t commit to : Alice can afford the risk of committing to high default demands (against both renegotiators and non-renegotiators). This is because she expects Bob might renegotiate, and thus the outcome of incompatible demands won’t be as bad. So, she’ll choose a default program that makes higher demands than she’d choose if Bob had committed to .
  • Bob therefore commits to to preempt such higher demands.

Various writings about SPIs have discussed similar problems before. But it’s important to spell this out carefully, because in my experience, looser discussions of this problem have led to confusions about the conditions necessary to avoid it. [9]

More general formulation. This first possibility encompasses any case where:

  1. Bob makes a commitment that leads him to not renegotiate with Alice (not just ); and
  2. Bob chooses this commitment for the following reason (at least partly): He thinks Alice will have an incentive to make higher demands because the SPI reduces her risk from higher demands, and he wants to remove this incentive, to the extent that he can do so.

When is this a problem?

Intuitively: At least as far as this first possibility goes, Bob only wants to opt out of renegotiation insofar as this makes a difference to Alice’s default demands . So, suppose Bob can commit to only renegotiate if Alice’s demands are no higher than if Bob had committed to never renegotiate. Then, in principle, Bob no longer has the above incentive to actually commit to never renegotiate. To be a bit more precise, let:

  • be the set of Bob programs that renegotiate only if , where
    • are the demands Alice would have made, had Bob committed to , i.e., to the analogous program in . (More details on what “would have” means in Appendix III.)

If , we say satisfies weak participation independence (PI). [10]

Then, the option of might block this first possibility: If Bob commits to , then by construction, he only renegotiates when he can verify that Alice’s demands aren’t worse for him than under . And, Bob would plausibly believe the following about Alice: She’ll anticipate Bob’s incentive to require weak PI. So, she won’t expect violating weak PI to pay off because renegotiation makes conflict less costly, since violating weak PI would disqualify her from renegotiation anyway. (Cf. the “non-punishment assumptions” discussed in Part II.1 of the agenda. [11] ) So Bob won’t prefer over for reason (2) listed in the “More general formulation” above.

However, suppose that at the time of bargaining, Alice can’t make credible that satisfies weak PI. Then even if Bob uses , he’ll still end up refusing to renegotiate with her. In practice, it might be infeasible for Alice to make weak PI credible, because this requires certifying a counterfactual.

Second possibility: Signaling aggressiveness

(This is less well-studied than the other mechanisms in this post, so take the following analysis as more uncertain.)

Above, we considered Alice’s incentive to make higher demands due to the SPI lowering the risk of such demands. Verifiable weak PI suffices for that problem. Here’s another worry: Suppose that when Bob chooses his commitment, he doesn’t yet know whether satisfies weak PI. Then from his perspective, Alice might still make higher demands if he commits to rather than (or some other commitment more stringent than ), based on what each commitment signals about him. This could give him a reason not to use , even if he could verify weak PI at the time of bargaining.

Specifically, suppose Bob expects Alice to learn whether he’s committed to or before she decides whether to commit to weak PI. Then Bob might imagine that, if he commits to , Alice will reason like this:

  • “What if I’d seen that Bob still wouldn’t renegotiate, even if I satisfy weak PI ()? That would be evidence that he’s irrational: he’d give up the opportunity to avoid pointless conflict, when this makes no difference to my demands.
  • “In that case, I’d be more worried about him rigidly committing to high demands, and commit to low demands myself (i.e., low ).
  • “But I know Bob is willing to sometimes renegotiate ()! So I’d rather violate weak PI and make higher demands than . Seems worth the risk that we end up fighting.”

So Bob might expect that committing to will signal that he’ll make high demands.

This isn’t to say the signal is strong evidence, or that it clearly goes in a direction that favors committing to . For example, insofar as Bob would consider it rational to make this commitment based on the argument above, then arguably, committing to can’t be strong evidence of “irrationality” in the first place! Or, committing to might just as well signal that Bob is unreasonably uncooperative, leading other agents to not trade with him. My claim is only that some agents might have an incentive to use for signaling purposes, if they’re willing to risk costly conflict.

When is this a problem?

The root of this problem is Bob’s uncertainty about whether Alice is committed to weak PI. If he decides whether to commit to after verifying that Alice has committed to weak PI, he has no incentive to commit to for signaling purposes. This is because in this case, he knows Alice would never demand less against than against , i.e., she wouldn’t respond favorably to the signal. But Bob might still prefer to commit to if he decides his commitment before verifying Alice’s commitment to weak PI. The analysis of when and why he might do so, in light of this post, is left as an exercise to the reader.

Third possibility: The SPI selection problem

So far, we’ve implicitly only considered a single SPI, namely, the mapping from to programs of the form in Algorithm 1 where:

  • and are the agents’ respective default programs;
  • line 5 of the algorithm also checks whether the other agent’s program satisfies weak PI; and
  • the agents’ renegotiation functions return matching proposals (line 5).

But, as originally discussed in Oesterheld & Conitzer (2022, Sec. 6), there can be a bargaining problem over multiple SPIs: the “SPI selection problem”. Specifically, Alice’s and Bob’s renegotiation functions might propose different outcomes, and their programs won’t necessarily agree on a proposal. The mechanistic explanation for this is very similar to the explanation for miscoordination in the agents’ original bargaining problem: Suppose Bob’s program conditions its proposed renegotiation outcome on incompatibility with Alice’s, i.e., backs down when their proposals don’t match. Then Alice’s program can insist on an outcome that’s better for her (and worse for Bob) risk-free. (And vice versa.) See also the table below.

Regular “equilibrium selection” problem (cf. Options 1 and 2 from “Taboo ‘equilibrium’”) SPI selection problem
There are a variety of commitments Bob could make to certain demands, which Alice would prefer to agree to rather than have bargaining fail — if she hasn’t committed otherwise. There are a variety of commitments Bob could make to certain renegotiation outcomes, which Alice would prefer to agree to rather than forgo the benefit of renegotiation — if she hasn’t committed otherwise.
But Alice might commit to not agree to those demands, because she expects Bob might be willing to back down to lower demands in response to her commitment. But Alice might commit to not agree to those renegotiation outcomes, because she expects Bob might be willing to back down to a renegotiation outcome that’s better for her in response to her commitment.
→ If Bob is committed to not back down, bargaining fails. → If Bob is committed to not back down, Bob doesn’t renegotiate.

When is this a problem?

It’s an open question whether, and how, the SPI selection problem can be solved or at least mitigated. Here’s a (non-exhaustive) survey of responses to the problem.

Alice verifiably commits “first”

Of course, if Alice commits to only accept a particular renegotiation outcome, and Bob verifies this before making an incompatible commitment, there’s no SPI selection problem. But the whole motivation for SPIs in the first place is that Alice and Bob might blindly commit to incompatible demands. So “just commit first” doesn’t seem to engage with the problem. [12]

Set-valued renegotiation and the “Pareto meet minimum”

Suppose, as in DiGiovanni et al. (2024), that each agent’s program can propose a set of renegotiation outcomes (see Algorithm 2 in Appendix IV). And suppose:

  1. Alice and Bob can at least agree on a function that selects an outcome from the intersection of their proposed sets (a “selection function”). So their programs renegotiate to that selected outcome, if the intersection is nonempty.
  2. The agents’ beliefs satisfy assumptions similar to those we invoked to argue that Bob might as well use rather than .
  3. They choose programs simultaneously.

Then, we can argue the following: Under the programs Alice and Bob individually prefer, they’ll at least renegotiate to an outcome no worse for either agent than the Pareto meet minimum (PMM), i.e., the payoff pair where each agent’s payoff is that of their least-preferred Pareto-efficient outcome. See Appendix IV for a (mostly) informal, corrected version of the paper’s argument for this result. Very briefly, the intuition is: Even though Bob has an incentive to insist on the best renegotiation outcome for himself, the PMM isn’t better for Alice than that outcome (by definition). So if he offers the PMM as well, Alice has no incentive to refuse his preferred outcome in order to get the PMM. (And the same holds switching the roles of Alice and Bob.)

But since writing that paper, I’m now significantly more worried that its argument for assumption (1) above doesn’t work (thanks to Nathaniel Sauerberg for raising this issue). I unpack this more in Appendix V, but roughly: The paper argues that agents can get the same outcome under any selection function by jointly switching their renegotiation sets. But we need each agent to expect the same outcomes by individually switching their set, and this seems to require strong assumptions.

“Dove-ish” renegotiation

Finally, consider this approach from Oesterheld & Conitzer (2022, Sec. 6):

[P]layers can profit from the use of SPIs even without addressing this SPI selection problem. To do so, a player picks an instruction that is very compliant (‘dove-ish’) w.r.t. what SPI is chosen, e.g., one that simply goes with whatever SPI the other players demand as long as that SPI cannot further be safely Pareto-improved upon.

In the context of renegotiation, such a “dove-ish” program would be a renegotiation program that matches whichever proposal Bob’s renegotiation function insists on, conditional on Bob satisfying weak PI.

To assess this idea, it’s helpful to separate two claims: 1) “Alice individually prefers to use a dove-ish program over any other renegotiation program.” 2) “Alice individually prefers to use a dove-ish program over a non-renegotiation program. And using a dove-ish program would significantly mitigate conflict, without being equivalent to just conceding to Bob’s demands.”

  • (1) seems false, for precisely the reasons given in the table above. So in that sense, dove-ish programs aren’t a solution to SPI selection.
  • But this need not imply that (2) is false. In particular, if Alice uses a dove-ish program, this would mitigate conflict without her needing to concede more than if she had never renegotiated.

Concluding thoughts on SPI selection

SPI selection currently seems like a serious conceptual challenge for SPIs. For example, it’s plausible that in order for the PMM argument to work, we’d need to basically assume away a fundamental bargaining problem (over selection functions). Another approach might be to argue that certain ways of resolving SPI selection are focal points. But I also find this unsatisfying, because the motivation for SPIs is that agents might fail to coordinate on a focal point in the first-order bargaining problem. (Though, coordinating on an SPI might still be easier in degree, even if the qualitative problem is the same as in first-order bargaining.)

However, I’m cautiously optimistic about a few directions for progress here.

First, even if DiGiovanni et al.’s argument as a whole fails, the argument that the PMM avoids perverse incentives does still seem sound. That is, the properties of the PMM itself are doing some work in the argument. So my intuition is that something like the PMM result might be provable under weaker assumptions than “the agents solve a bargaining problem that’s just as hard as the original problem”.

Second (h/t Nathaniel Sauerberg): Consider SPIs implemented via delegating to an agent with different goals, but with the twist that this delegate can itself implement another delegation-based SPI. Then the delegate themselves faces an SPI selection problem, not just the original agent. So if SPI selection breaks down, the downsides might fall on the delegate’s goals rather than the original agent’s. (There’s a lot more to say on this idea, which I leave to future work, but that’s the basic sketch.)

Lastly, a promising approach is to have “our” AIs err somewhat on the side of caution at the level of choosing an SPI, while still allowing them to be more or less assertive in first-order bargaining. Dove-ish renegotiation is one instance of this. While it’s possible that we’ll conclude this strategy is too conservative, it seems well-motivated under severe uncertainty about what kinds of SPIs others might accept.
